CASE REPORT:

MAQ, a 50-year-old male, was first seen
in the outpatient clinic at Aga Khan University Hospital in 1988, complaining of low
back pain radiating to the thighs, persistent
for the last four years. The pain was gradually
progressive, increasing on exertion and bending. There was no particular dermatomal
distribution of pain. X-rays of the lumbosacral spine were negative and neurological
examinations were usually reported as unremarkable. He was advised to take regular

back strengthening exercises, along with
analgesics. The response to these measures,
however, was poor.

On examination, mild spasm was noted
in the paraspinal muscles of the lumbar regions bilaterally. Neurological examination
was essentially unremarkable. He was advised admission, which he refused.

He returned back in October 1989 with
increased pain in the back, which also spread
anteriorly in the thoracic region as well as the
abdomen. He would also have occasional
spasms on exertion. The complaints had
gradually butsignificantly increased over the
last one year. On examination, he had increased tone in both the lower limbsas well as
the upper limbs. Reflexes were mildly brisk,
plantar responses were flexor. The SLR was
60°. He was admitted for investigations.

The routine biochemical investigations
were normal. ESR was 15mm at 1 hour. CPK
was 40 IU (30-176). A myelogram along with
myelo-CT studies did not reveal any significant abnormality. EMG and nerve conduction studies were essentially normal. A provisional diagnosis of some kind of progressive
myelopathy of unknown etiology was made.
He was advised to take tablet lioresal
(baclofen), analgesics etc., as well as regular
physiotherapy, and follow up in the clinic.

He was lost to follow up for the next
three years. He came back in September 1992

with marked worsening of symptoms,
marked increased in pain and stiffness, and
marked spasms on exertion. As a result, his
physical activity was considerably restricted.
The spasms involved the trunk as well as
limbs. He reported that he used to feel better
whenever he took tablet baclofen.

On examination, there was marked rigidity all over, including board like rigidity
of the abdominal muscles. There were spasms
of the back muscles, with lordosis. Reflexes
were normal and the plantar responses were
flexor. Sensory examination was normal. An
EMG done at this stage showed continuous
activity of the muscles at rest. The motor
units were normal, no denervation activity
was seen. Nerve conduction velocities were
normal.

Based on the clinical history and the EMG
and nerve conduction findings, a diagnosis of
stiff-man syndrome was made. He was
started on tablet diazepam 5 mg 3 times a
day. Marked improvement in his symptoms
was noted in the first week. Over the next few
wecks, the dose of diazepam was gradually
increased to 15 mg 3 times a day and he
continued toimprove over this period. At the
end of 4 weeks, he could perform most of his
previous activities with relative ease. His
examination at the end of four months revealed a power of grade 5, with normal reflexes. Only mild rigidity was noted over the
abdominal muscles.

His symptoms continued to remain under
control on treatment with tablet diazepam.
Atlast attendance in October 1993, he continued to remain stable and was ambulatory.
The dose of diazepam required to control his
symptoms was around 40 to 50 mgs per day.

DISCUSSION
Stiff-man syndrome (or stiff-person

syndrome) is a rare disorder of motor function, characterised by involuntary stiffness of

250

axial muscles, and superimposed by painful

muscles spasms, which are often induced by

startle, or cmotional stimuli. The disorder
usually responds to benzodiapenes.?

This disorder was first reported in 1956
by Moersch and Woltman?, who reported
their experience with 14 patients with involuntary stiffness of the axial musculature
and superimposed muscle spasms. No underlying neurological or other causes were
discovered to explain these findings, so the
entity was named stiff-man syndrome.

The diagnostic criteria used by Lorish et
al., in their analysis of 13 patients included
the following:!

1. A prodrome of stiffness and rigidity in
axial muscles.

2. Slow progression of stiffness to include

proximal limb muscles making volitional

movements and ambulation difficult.

A fixed deformity of the spine.

4. The presence of superimposed episodic
spasms precipitated by sudden movement, jarring, noise, and emotional upsets.

5. Normal findings on motor and sensory
nerve examination.

6. Normal intellect.

7. Typical electromyographic finding of
continuous motor activity abolished by
the intravenous administration of diazepam, or a positive response to a therapeutic of trial of orally administered
diazepam.

In their analysis of these 13 patients, the
authors found that muscle rigidity and spasms
were mainly noted in back muscles, abdominal muscles and lower extremities, with few
patients having spasms of the muscles of the
head and neck. Except for muscle rigidity and
spasms, there are no other abnormal neurological findings. Hyperlordosis may be seen
in some cases.

Our patient satisfied all the criteria
mentioned above. A noteworthy feature of

w

his illness has been that his symptoms persisted for well over 8 years, before a definite
diagnosis of stiff-man syndrome could be
made. This has been the experience of others
too,’ and since, because of its rare occurrence, and also because of its findings of
rigidity and stiffness, stiff-man syndrome is
at times misdiagnosed, unless carefully
looked for, and highly suspected. Many
neurologic and psychiatric conditions may
mimic stiff-man syndrome, including chronic
tetanus, some forms of chronic progressive
myelopathy, extra-pyramidal syndromes,
inflammatory myopathics, and conditions
giving rest to continuous muscles activity of
peripheral nerve origin i.e. Issacs syndrome,
muscle cramps, etc.’ The diagnosis therefore
is, based on identification of the positive
symptomsand signs, as well as the absence of
other causes which could cause the same
clinical features.

The pathophysiological basis of stiff-man
syndrome is not very clear. Thisis probably a
disorder of the Renshaw cells, causing loss of
inhibition of motor neurons, resulting and
rigidity and spasms.*4 Later, Gordon and
colleagues proposed that there may be abnormal function of the gamma motor neuron
fibers which increase the muscle tone through
muscle spindles.* A disorder of brain-stem
regulated neurotransmitter system has been
proposed by some authors.®’ There appears
to be an increase in the excitatory aminergic
(nor-adrenergic and serotonergic) activity in
the central nervous system, and a reduction
in the inhibitory GABA activity. Thus, drugs
that increase aminergic activity in the CNS
(levodopa, clompramine, reserpine etc.)
would increase the severity of spasms, whilst
drugs that enhance GABA activity (baclofens
or benzodiazepenes) would diminish the
spasms.’

Itisnow widely believed, that stiff-man
syndrome is most likely an autoimmune
disease. In 1988, Solimena and his co-workers

251

Stiff-man syndrome
reported the presence of antibodies directed
at glutamic acid decarboxylase in the serum
and cerebrospinal fluid of a patient stiff-man
syndrome, type I diabetes mellitus and
epilepsy.’ Although the pathogenic significance of the antibodies could not be inferred
from these findings, the presence of antibody
in this patient, and the frequentassociation of
organ-specific autoimmune endocrinopathies in this and other patients with the clinical
diagnosis of the stiff-man syndrome suggest
thatstiff-man syndrome is indeed anautoimmune process. Jn a recent report, the same
investigators have described finding antiglutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies in
the serum of 22 of the 33 patients clinically
diagnosed as having stiff-man syndrome.
The organ specific autoimmune diseases that
tend to occur in families and patients of stiffman syndrome include pernicious anemia,
thyroiditis, adernalitis, hypoparathyroiditism, myasthenia gravis, diabetes mellitus,
ovarian failure, vitiligo etc."

Most patients respond symptomatically
to diazepam, the normal dose requirements
being around 20 to 40 mg daily. Upto 300 mgs
have been administered in resistant cases.*5
Other drugs thathavebeen found tobe useful
are tablet lioresal (baclofen), valproic acid,
clonazepam etc.’2"*4 It is also to be noted that
drugs that increase the nor-adrenergic and
serotonergic activity would worsen symptoms of stiff-man syndrome. Thus, L. Dopa,
reserpine clomipramine etc are to be avoided $

Aninteresting development has been the
use of immunosuppression with or without
plasmapharesis in stiff-man syndrome.'®6
Improvement has been reported in some
cases, 16 but not in others.!”

In most patients there is usually a gradual progression in the severity of the symptoms. However, patients are ambulatory on
increasing dosages of diazepam. Before the
discovery that diazepam was an effective
treatment for stiff-man syndrome, many

patients were totally bedbound and disabled.
Interestingly, sedation does not occur as a
regular side-effect. Diazepam induced depression may be a problem in others." The
long-term effects of steroids and plasmapharesis have not been evaluated in this
condition, given the rarity of the disorder.

Although stiff-man syndrome is a rare
disorder, a positive diagnosis can usually be
made with a high index of suspicion, and a
careful exclusion of other diseases. Given the
fact that most cases of stiff-man syndrome
can now be fairly well controlled with medications, itis important to make every effort to
arrive at a positive diagnosis.
